title: MB8-24790
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She appeals a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision dated November 5, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant is a citizen of Nigeria from Lagos. She appeals a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision dated November 5, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection. She is requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the RPD's negative determination and find that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, she asks that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. She has not requested to submit new evidence or to hold an oral hearing.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 BACKGROUND Basis of Claim

The appellant alleges that she is bisexual and that she fears death at the hands of an anti-gay vigilante group in Nigeria. The rest of the central allegations are summarized by the RPD in the summary of allegations section of its decision.2 RPD Decision
The RPD rejected the claim because it found the central allegations not credible.

Given the documented level of homophobia in Nigerian society, the RPD found it implausible that E, a Nigerian lesbian, would accept an invitation from an anti-gay vigilante group to attend at a certain place, at a certain time. It therefore drew a negative inference.

Even if they had made a public announcement about N's sexual orientation, the RPD found it implausible that the anti-gay vigilante group could have intercepted N on her way to the airport. The RPD found it unlikely that they would have known that N was travelling to the airport when she did, considering that Nigeria is a country of 180 million people and she had previously been in hiding in several different parts of the country. The RPD therefore drew another negative inference.

The RPD did not believe that the appellant went into hiding in different places after XXXX 2015 because, contrary to her testimony and her BOC, her claim intake documents3 indicated that she stayed at the same address, in the same town, and did the same job over this period, and she was not able to provide a reasonable explanation for the discrepancies. The RPD rejected her explanation that she did not know the exact address of the places she hid because she did not even indicate that she was living in different towns over this period in her claim intake documents. It also rejected her explanation that she put the contents that she did in her claim intake documents for this period of time only to obtain a visa to Canada. The RPD noted that claim intake forms are not executed for visitor visa purposes, that the appellant understands English, and had been in Canada for years by the time she signed them. The RPD therefore drew a further negative inference.

The RPD found that her registration at a university in Canada in XXXX 2014 was inconsistent with her allegation that her family only retained an agent to help her get a student visa to Canada to enable her to leave Nigeria in XXXX 2014. The RPD rejected her explanation that her father may have made unknown efforts on his own to get her out of Nigeria before then because, according to her allegations, her need to leave Nigeria did not arise until XXXX 2014. The RPD therefore drew a further negative inference.

In the context of her allegations, the RPD found it implausible that she would have waited XXXX months after arriving in Canada in XXXX 2015 to claim asylum in Canada which she ultimately did in August 2017. It therefore drew yet another negative inference.

The RPD placed no weight on her mother's letter4 as proof of the central allegations because it found that the appellant was not a credible or trustworthy witness and the appellant had provided the letter.

In rendering this appeal decision, the RAD has considered Chairperson's Guideline 9.5 The RAD has also done an independent assessment of the record. The RAD is reviewing the RPD decision on a standard of correctness. Determinative Issue
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the RPD erred in assessing the appellant's credibility. For the following reasons and having examined the record and assessed it independently, the RAD finds that it concurs with the RPD and that there is insufficient credible evidence upon which to determine the appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Benefit of the Doubt

The appellant submits that the RPD erred in failing to accord the appellant the benefit of the doubt. The RAD rejects this submission. The RAD and the RPD started from the presumption of truth but they have both found it rebutted by the problems with the appellants' evidence discussed below. Bisexuality requires protection even if it is not credible

The appellant submits that the RPD should have granted the appellant protection based on her bisexuality even if it did not believe her. The RAD rejects this submission. The appellant does not need protection if she is not bisexual and the allegations are not true, on a balance of probabilities. E's Death

The appellant submits that the RPD should not have found it implausible that E, a Nigerian lesbian, would accept an invitation from an anti-gay vigilante group to attend at a certain place at a certain time. The RAD rejects this submission and concurs with the RPD's finding. The RAD finds it implausible that E, a Nigerian lesbian, would accept an invitation from an anti-gay vigilante group to attend at a certain place at a certain time given the widespread and well-known levels of homophobia in Nigeria. The RAD therefore draws a negative inference as to the appellant's credibility as witness and the central allegations in the case. N's Death

The appellant submits that the RPD should not have relied on the implausibility finding it made here because her death was a peripheral matter. The RAD rejects this submission. In the RAD's view, N's death is not peripheral; it is one of the central allegations. Moreover, the RAD agrees with the RPD's finding that it is implausible that an anti-gay vigilante group could have intercepted her at the precise time she chose to travel to the airport. The RAD therefore draws another negative inference as to the appellant's credibility as a witness and the central allegations in the case. Her Father's Death

The appellant submits that the RPD should not have found the appellant to be speculating that her father was killed by the anti-gay vigilantes, and should have accorded her the benefit of the doubt as to the cause of his death even if the death certificates are not reliable. The RAD rejects this submission. The RAD and the RPD started from the presumption of truth but they have both found it rebutted by the problems with the appellants' evidence discussed herein. Furthermore, the RAD concurs with the RPD regarding the contents of the death certificates.6 They do conflict as to where he lived and where his death was registered. The RAD therefore places no weight on them as proof of the cause of his death. Given what the country documents say about the extent and frequency of crime in Nigeria,7 the RAD concurs with the RPD that it was speculative for the appellant to conclude that the anti-gay vigilantes killed her father. The RAD therefore draws another negative inference as to the appellant's credibility as a witness and the central allegations in the case. Hiding

The appellant submits that the RPD was hostile when it concluded that the claim intake forms are not student visa forms and that the appellant's explanation that she only provided the contents for a visa purpose was therefore unreasonable. The RAD rejects this submission and concurs with the RPD that this is an unreasonable explanation for the discrepancies between these forms and the appellant's other evidence as to her whereabouts after XXXX 2015. Claim intake forms are not executed to obtain visas to Canada. The RAD therefore draws another negative inference as to the appellant's credibility and the central allegations in the case. Delay in Claiming

The appellant submits that the RPD erred in rejecting the appellant's explanation for the delay which was that she was waiting for time to pass in the hope that the anti-gay vigilantes might forget about her, and that she finally realized she had to claim when N was killed in XXXX 2017. The RAD accepts this submission. While it is not determinative of the appeal, the RAD's independent assessment of the record indicates that the RPD erred in finding this period of time to constitute a delay in claiming. An entry stamp8 on the appellant's passport indicates that the she was given leave to remain until XXXX XXXX, 2019, when she entered Canada and she therefore had no prior need to claim asylum. The appellant therefore committed no delay in failing to initiate her refugee protection claim until August 2017. However, and again, given the other negative credibility findings made, this error is not determinative. The rest of the RPD findings

The rest of the RPD's reasons for disbelieving the appellant were not challenged by the appellants and the RAD finds that it concurs with the RPD with respect to them. The RAD therefore draws a final negative inference as to the appellant's credibility as a witness and the central allegations in the case.

Except for the one erroneous finding about her delay in claiming, which I have found is not determinative of this appeal, the RAD rejects the appellant's submissions. The RAD finds that it concurs with the rest of the RPD's analysis and the multiple reasons it provided for disbelieving the central allegations in the case.

The RAD therefore finds that the appellant is not a credible or trustworthy witness and that the central allegations in this case, including the appellant's alleged bisexuality, are not true, on a balance of probabilities.
The RAD therefore finds that it has insufficient credible evidence upon which to determine the appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

The RAD therefore finds that the appellant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground and, on a balance of probabilities, that she would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she returned to Nigeria.

The RAD therefore dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the appellant is a neither Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. (signed) "Joel Bousfield" Joel Bousfield November 13, 2019 Date 1 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, as amended. 2 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Record, RPD Reasons, at pp. 3-4. 3 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Record, Exhibit 2, at pp. 24-38. 4 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Record, Exhibit 2, at p. 59. 5 Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB), Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings before the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression, May 1, 2017 6 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Record, Exhibit 2, at pp. 51 and 58. 7 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD's Record, Exhibit 3, National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria (July 10, 2018), See all items in section 7; Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Record, RPD Reasons, at p. 20. 8 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Record, Exhibit 2, at p. 41. --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ RAD File / Dossier de la SAR : MB8-24790 RAD.25.02 (April 04, 2019) Disponible en français 8 Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada Refugee Appeal Division Commission de l'immigration et du statut de réfugié du Canada Section d'appel des réfugiés RAD.25.02 (April 04, 2019) Disponible en français
